blocks.text: A catalytic converter is a ceramic or metallic monolith with a honeycomb-like structure, as shown in Figure 12.6. Its inner channels have a layer of alumina to provide a high surface area. Noble expensive metals such as Pt (Platinum), Pd (Palladium), and Rh (Rhodium) are dispersed on the alumina.

These metals catalyze three redox reactions to remove the half harmful exhaust gases. The three-way converter converts harmful CO, NO, and hydrocarbons into CO₂, N₂, and water. These precious metals can also be recycled.

blocks.alt: Cut-away view of a catalytic converter: an outlet pipe on the left, a wider metal body holding two honeycomb monolith blocks, and an inlet pipe on the right. Thick yellow arrows show HC, CO, NOx entering at the lower right, passing through the honeycomb and leaving at the upper left as H2O, CO2, N2. A leader line points into a block with the label 'washcoat with catalyst inside the monolith channel'.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.6: Three-way catalytic converter (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.6).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: ‘Rd’ is not the symbol of any element. The catalyst is platinum/rhodium, Pt/Rh, as printed for the oxidation of CO.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Here too ‘Rd’ should be Rh: the catalyst is Pt/Rh.
